techniques.name: GNNExplainer
techniques.description: GNNExplainer explains one prediction of a graph neural network, a model that passes information along the edges of a graph such as a molecule, a payment network or a mesh of weather grid points, by finding a small subgraph and a small set of input features that most support that prediction. Explanation methods for flat inputs, such as SHAP and LIME, give each input feature its own score and have no built-in notion of a connection between two nodes; this method scores the connections themselves, restricted to the part of the graph the model actually reads for the prediction (its computation graph, the neighbourhood within as many hops as the model has message-passing layers). It learns a mask with a value between 0 and 1 for each edge of that computation graph and for each node-feature dimension by gradient descent: the masked graph is fed to the model, and the masks are adjusted to keep the predicted label as likely as possible while penalties keep the total mask small and push values towards 0 or 1. Edges and features whose mask values fall below a threshold are then dropped, leaving a compact subgraph and feature subset that can be drawn over the input graph; the same procedure explains node labels, predicted links and whole-graph labels, and the original paper also aligns the explanations of many nodes of one class into a summary pattern. It needs gradient access to the model, and each explanation is a separate optimisation.

example_use_cases.description: A pharmaceutical company's computational toxicology team uses a graph neural network to flag candidate molecules as likely mutagenic. For each flagged compound it reviews the substructure and atom features GNNExplainer selects and checks them against known structural alerts such as nitro groups, to decide whether a flag rests on chemistry the team recognises before the compound is deprioritised.

A bank's financial-crime unit scores accounts with a graph neural network over its payment network to flag likely money-mule accounts. Investigators receive with each flag the explanation subgraph of counterparties and transfers and the account features it selected, and use them to decide whether to escalate; model validators sample explanations to check that flags do not rest mainly on features such as branch or account-opening channel.

A weather service's model evaluation team runs the regression mode of the PyTorch Geometric implementation on a small set of high-impact forecasts from a graph-based forecasting model, such as the predicted rainfall total at one location. Forecasters check whether the connections and input variables selected, for example humidity upwind, are physically plausible, and the team deletes the selected connections to confirm the forecast changes, before such forecasts feed a warning service.

limitations.description: Each explanation is a separate optimisation, run for a set number of steps (100 by default in the PyTorch Geometric implementation), so explaining many nodes or graphs is slow and explanations of similar cases are not required to agree. A view of the model as a whole needs an extra step, such as the class-level summary in the original paper, or a method that trains one explainer for all instances.

The masks are soft during optimisation, so the model is run on graphs whose edges and features are scaled by fractions it never saw in training, and these values can add meaning or noise of their own. The objective is not convex and the masks start at random: in a 2024 benchmark, the ten-edge explanations from runs with different seeds overlapped by a Jaccard index of only 0.18 to 0.80 across six datasets. The final subgraph also depends on the threshold used to cut the mask.

The size of the explanation is set by the user, not found. The original experiments fixed it at the known size of the planted pattern on synthetic graphs and at 10 edges and 5 features on real ones, and the PyTorch Geometric implementation advises tuning the size penalty to the graph's average degree. A compact explanation can therefore leave out structure the model uses.

Most evidence that it finds the right structure comes from synthetic graphs with planted patterns, and a trained model need not use the planted edges, so agreement with them can mislead. A 2023 benchmark found graph explainers, this one included, less faithful when linked nodes tend to differ and when the deciding structure is large. Check fidelity on your own model, for example by deleting the explanation and measuring the change.

It assumes the computation graph is small. The computation graph grows with every message-passing layer, so in a mesh-based forecasting model that passes messages many times along long-range edges (GraphCast uses 16 such layers) it probably spans most of the mesh: the mask then covers most edges and compactness comes from the size penalty, not the model. This has not been tested. PyTorch Geometric applies the mask inside its own message-passing layers, so the model must use them or be adapted.

resources.title: GNNExplainer: Generating Explanations for Graph Neural Networks
resources.abstract:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a powerful tool for machine learning on graphs.GNNs combine node feature information with the graph structure by 
recursively passing neural messages along edges of the input graph. However, incorporating both graph structure and feature information leads to complex models,
and explaining predictions made by GNNs remains unsolved. Here
we propose GNNExplainer, the first general, model-agnostic approach for providing interpretable explanations for predictions of any GNN-based model on any graph-based machine learning task. Given an instance, GNNExplainer identifies a compact subgraph structure and a small subset of node features that have a crucial role in GNN's prediction. 
Further, GNNExplainer  can generate consistent and concise explanations for an entire class of instances.
We formulate GNNExplainer as an optimization task that maximizes the mutual information between a GNN's prediction and distribution of possible subgraph structures. Experiments on synthetic and real-world graphs show that our approach can identify important graph structures as well as node features, and outperforms baselines by 17.1% on average. GNNExplainer  provides a variety of benefits, from the ability to visualize semantically relevant structures to interpretability, to giving insights into errors of faulty GNNs.

techniques.name: Sparse Autoencoder Feature Analysis
techniques.description: Sparse autoencoder feature analysis looks for human-interpretable units inside a neural network, usually a language model, by learning from the activations at one layer a large dictionary of directions, called features, such that each activation vector can be rebuilt from only a few of them. Unlike neuron activation analysis it does not take the network's own neurons as the units, since single neurons often respond to several unrelated things, and unlike concept activation vectors it needs no labelled examples of a concept chosen in advance, because the features are found without supervision. The analyst records activations at the chosen layer over a large body of ordinary text and trains an autoencoder, a network with one hidden layer usually several times wider than the layer studied, to reconstruct them while a sparsity penalty keeps most hidden units at zero; the decoder weights of each hidden unit then give one feature direction. Each feature is labelled from the inputs on which it fires most strongly, by a person or by a language model that writes a description, which is then scored on how well it predicts the feature's activations on other text, and the label is tested by removing or amplifying the feature inside the running model and checking the change in output. The output is a catalogue of labelled features with example activations, interpretability scores and measured effects, plus a reconstruction score saying how much of the layer's behaviour the dictionary accounts for; the features can then serve as units for causal mediation analysis, which traces pathways, while this method finds and checks the units themselves.

example_use_cases.description: Before deploying an open-weights language model as a customer-service assistant, a bank's AI assurance team uses sparse autoencoders published for that model to find features active on prompts where the assistant should refuse to give investment advice. It tests each candidate by suppressing it and measuring the change in refusal rate, and records which labelled features the refusal behaviour depends on in the model's assurance file.

A bioinformatics group using a protein language model to annotate newly sequenced proteins trains sparse autoencoders on its embeddings and compares the features with database annotations of binding sites, structural motifs and domains. Features that match known biology are used to propose candidate annotations for curators to verify, features that fire widely with no clear meaning are flagged for review, and the model's own annotation accuracy is still tested on held-out proteins.

A team that fine-tuned a language model to triage clinical referral letters lists the sparse autoencoder features that most change the 'urgent' score on a validation set, and checks whether they describe clinical content or properties of the letter, such as the referring practice's template. A template feature among the leading drivers is recorded as a finding and leads to retraining on reformatted letters.

limitations.description: The dictionary does not capture everything the layer carries, and what it misses cannot be inspected. In the originating study, replacing one layer of a small language model with its reconstruction raised perplexity from 25 to 40; a concurrent study recovered 79% of a layer's contribution to the loss in its main run. Not finding a feature for a concept does not show that the model lacks it.

The features found are not unique. Larger dictionaries split a feature into narrower ones (one base64 feature at 512 features became three at 4,096), and for a 131,000-feature autoencoder on one layer of Llama 3 8B only about 30% of features were shared by two runs differing only in random seed. A conclusion resting on one feature should name the autoencoder used and be checked on a second run.

Labels are hypotheses drawn from the top-activating examples, and automated scores are modest: the first five features reported in the originating study scored between -0.11 and 0.57, and the advantage over simpler decompositions faded in later layers. Back a label with an intervention that changes the output as the label predicts before citing it as evidence.

It needs the model's internal activations, plus storage and compute to train an autoencoder for each layer studied (one concurrent study trained on 8 billion activation vectors from a single layer). For large models practitioners often rely on autoencoders released for particular open-weights models, so the method is not available for a model reached only through an API.

Being interpretable does not make the features better for a given task. In a 2025 study of detecting concepts from model activations, probes built on autoencoder features did not beat logistic regression on the raw activations on average, and the spurious correlations and data problems they exposed could also be found with simpler baselines. Where detection is the goal, compare against such baselines.

techniques.name: AI FactSheets
techniques.description: AI FactSheets is a documentation practice in which the developer or supplier of an AI model or service answers a structured set of questions about it, modelled on the supplier's declarations of conformity that industries such as telecommunications and transport use to give written assurance, with evidence, that a product meets stated requirements. The questions cover the service's purpose and its intended and unsuitable uses, the datasets it was trained and tested on, its test methods and results (reported for groups such as age bands or genders where relevant), checks for bias, explainability, behaviour on data unlike its training data and robustness to adversarial attack, how user data is secured, and its lineage, such as when and how its models were retrained; 'N/A' and 'Proprietary' are allowed answers. Facts are gathered from the people in each role across the lifecycle (business owner, data scientist, model validator and operations engineer), and any change to the service produces a new version of the FactSheet while earlier versions are kept. The originating group's seven-step method designs the template with its readers: interview the people who will read the facts and those who will produce them, draft and trial a template of questions, have the real producers complete it, evaluate the result with its readers for content and presentation, and build further templates for other audiences such as a review board or regulator. Unlike a model card, which reports one model's intended use and evaluation to the people choosing it, or a datasheet, which describes one dataset, a FactSheet may cover one model or a whole service built from several models and datasets (attaching their datasheets), gathers facts from each role in the lifecycle and has a different template for each audience; unlike a CycloneDX ML-BOM it is written for people to read rather than as a machine-readable parts list for software tools.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital trust buying a speech-to-text service for clinical dictation sends bidders a FactSheet template asking for intended and unsuitable uses, training data, retraining frequency, behaviour on noisy audio, and word error rates by speaker accent and age band on recordings the trust supplies. The panel compares the answers to shortlist bidders, re-tests the shortlisted services on its own recordings, and writes the confirmed error rates into the contract as service levels.

A bank's model risk team follows the seven-step method to design a FactSheet template for credit models: it interviews validators about the decisions they make and data scientists about the facts they can record, then has the scientists complete it for a new affordability model. Validators read the completed FactSheet's training data, performance, bias checks and known weak cases before deciding whether to approve the model for deployment.

A company selling a sentiment-analysis API publishes a short FactSheet for developers browsing its catalogue, giving the purpose, input and output formats, training data, accuracy and the kinds of text the service handles poorly. From the same facts it generates a longer FactSheet, with a different template, for enterprise customers' risk and compliance reviewers.

A city council's AI ethics review board asks each supplier for a FactSheet in a template written for the board, covering training and test data distributions, data handling, the inputs the service handles poorly and possible sources of unfair outcomes. The board reads them before deciding whether a photo-based street-repair reporting service may go live.

limitations.description: A FactSheet is the supplier's own declaration. As with the declarations of conformity it imitates, the supplier runs the tests it reports and nothing in the format checks them, so it shows what was claimed rather than that the claims hold. A buyer who relies on a declared figure has to re-test the service or ask for third-party testing, which the original proposal expects only for the highest-stakes, regulated, enterprise and public-sector applications.

Facts not recorded while the service is built are hard to recover. In IBM's own trials, developers forgot how they had transformed training data or which settings they had tried, and recovering the training-data transformations for one FactSheet took several hours over two days although the dataset was small and its author was available. A FactSheet written after development is likely to have gaps or errors unless fact collection is part of the development process.

The format accepts 'N/A' and 'Proprietary' as answers. In IBM's trials most developers assumed bias would not be an issue and marked bias questions not applicable, even where further questioning showed it could be, and participants were unsure how much detail they could give without losing competitive advantage. An unchallenged 'N/A' can hide a risk nobody examined, and items withheld as proprietary are often the ones a buyer would need in order to check the self-declared results.

There is no single FactSheet. Its authors hold that one template cannot serve every audience and domain, and developers report the metrics conventional for their kind of model, so FactSheets from different suppliers often cannot be compared unless the buyer fixes the questions, metrics and test conditions in its own template.

Whether readers understand FactSheets and decide better with them is untested. Producers in IBM's studies found it hard to know what readers needed and often left out what a less expert reader would need. The design method checks a draft with a few intended readers, and the group's later case studies report that producers could follow it, but none of these sources tests whether buyers, validators or review boards read FactSheets correctly or make better decisions with them.

resources.title: A Methodology for Creating AI FactSheets
resources.abstract: As AI models and services are used in a growing number of highstakes areas, a consensus is forming around the need for a clearer record of how these models and services are developed to increase trust. Several proposals for higher quality and more consistent AI documentation have emerged to address ethical and legal concerns and general social impacts of such systems. However, there is little published work on how to create this documentation. This is the first work to describe a methodology for creating the form of AI documentation we call FactSheets. We have used this methodology to create useful FactSheets for nearly two dozen models. This paper describes this methodology and shares the insights we have gathered. Within each step of the methodology, we describe the issues to consider and the questions to explore with the relevant people in an organization who will be creating and consuming the AI facts in a FactSheet. This methodology will accelerate the broader adoption of transparent AI documentation.

techniques.name: UK Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard Record
techniques.description: An Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS) record is a public account that a UK public sector organisation writes about one algorithmic tool it uses, on the UK government's standard template, and publishes in a central repository on GOV.UK. The template has two tiers: a short plain-language summary for the general public (what the tool is, why it is used and a contact), and eight further sheets for specialist readers such as journalists, researchers and civil society, covering who is accountable for the tool and which suppliers were involved, how it works and what it replaced, how its output feeds into decisions, when a person reviews that output, how members of the public can appeal, the system's and each model's inputs, outputs, architecture and performance (including any bias testing), the data used, and the impact assessments, risks and mitigations. Information that would be exempt under the Freedom of Information Act can be left out or summarised field by field, with the reason stated, and the record is cleared by the tool's team, its senior responsible owner (the role accountable for the tool) and the press office, checked for readability by the central ATRS team, and updated when the tool changes substantially or is retired. Publishing is mandatory for central government departments and for arm's-length bodies that deliver public or frontline services or deal directly with the public, for tools in beta, pilot or production that significantly influence decisions affecting the public or interact with it directly; other public bodies may publish voluntarily. Unlike a model card, written by a developer for people choosing a model, or a supplier's AI FactSheet for buyers, an ATRS record is written by the deploying public body for the public and describes the decision process, human review and appeal routes around the tool as well as the tool.

example_use_cases.description: A government department piloting a machine-learning model that prioritises benefit claims for caseworker checks publishes an ATRS record before the pilot starts. It tells claimants, journalists and MPs that the score only orders the caseworkers' queue and a caseworker makes every decision, how claimants can ask for a review, what kinds of data the model uses and what bias testing was done.

A district council piloting a supplier's tool that ranks rent-arrears cases for housing officers publishes a voluntary ATRS record. Because the record needs the model type, a description of the training data and performance figures, the council's procurement team writes their supply into the contract, and the record names the supplier, its role and the terms of its access to tenants' data.

A police force using a domestic-abuse risk assessment tool publishes a voluntary record in which the fields that would show how to evade the tool are marked exempt, with the reason, while the summary, the officers' review of each score, the appeal route and the risk mitigations are published in full for oversight bodies and community groups to examine.

A department launching a chatbot that answers questions about a public service publishes a record because the tool interacts directly with the public. The record states that answers come from a named provider's large language model used as supplied, how answers are checked, how often conversations are reviewed and how a user reaches a human adviser.

limitations.description: A record is the deploying body's own account. The central ATRS team checks drafts for readability, not accuracy, and nothing in the standard tests the stated performance, bias testing or human review against the tool's behaviour. A record is also only as current as its last update, which depends on the body resubmitting after a substantial change, so it shows what was disclosed and when, not that the tool works as described.

The mandatory scope is narrow: central government departments and qualifying arm's-length bodies, and only tools that significantly influence decisions with public effect or interact directly with the public, from the beta or pilot stage on. Local authorities, police forces and other bodies outside central government publish voluntarily, and analytical models that inform policy are usually out of scope, so the absence of a record does not show that no tool is in use.

Fields can be withheld or summarised under Freedom of Information exemptions, including commercial interests, and no record is published where even the tool's existence cannot be confirmed. Police and commercial interviewees in a 2022 study expected suppliers to resist disclosing proprietary details, so the technical tier of a record for a procured tool can be thin unless the contract requires the supplier to provide the information.

For an off-the-shelf model that the organisation has not trained, tested or refined, such as a large language model used through its web interface, the guidance says to leave the model and development data sections blank. Records for such tools say nothing about the model's training data or evaluation, which is often what a reader most needs in order to judge them.

Whether the public can find, understand and use records has not been tested. Records sit in a repository on GOV.UK rather than reaching people when a decision affects them, although the 2021 public engagement study behind the two-tier design found people wanted active notice for higher-impact uses. Police interviewees in a 2022 study feared records would give more detail than the public needs and accuracy figures without context; its authors called for evaluation with impacted communities.

techniques.name: C2PA Content Credentials
techniques.description: C2PA Content Credentials attach a signed provenance record, called a manifest, to a media file, so that whoever receives the file can see who signed it and what the signer declares (which tool produced it, whether a generative AI model created or altered it and what edits followed), and can check that the record, and the parts of the file its hash covers, have not changed since signing. Under the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) technical specification, the tool that creates or edits the file writes statements called assertions, such as a 'created' action whose source type is trainedAlgorithmicMedia (the code for AI-generated content) and links to the earlier files it was made from, adds a cryptographic hash of the file's content, and signs the bundle with an X.509 certificate, the kind of credential used to secure websites. The manifest is usually embedded in the file, and each later edit in a supporting tool adds a new manifest that refers to the previous one, so the history travels with the file. A validator recomputes the hash and checks the signature, then reports the manifest as well-formed, valid or, if the signing certificate chains to a trust list such as the C2PA Trust List, trusted, and reports a failure when the file no longer matches its hash. If the manifest is removed, nothing in the file leads back to it unless a watermark or fingerprint (a 'soft binding') was also registered so that the manifest can be looked up in a repository, and a file without credentials says nothing about its origin; unlike trigger-set model watermarking or model signing, which mark or sign a model, it records the history of an individual output.

example_use_cases.description: An image-generation service offered in the EU attaches a signed manifest to every image it returns, declaring an AI 'created' action with the service as signer, as its means of meeting the AI Act's Article 50(2) duty to mark synthetic output in a machine-readable format. Its compliance team validates a weekly sample of outputs to decide whether marking is working, and registers a watermark soft binding so that a stripped image can be matched back to its record.

A news agency's verification desk runs every image sent in by the public through a C2PA validator before publication. A trusted manifest recording capture on a named camera, with no AI-generated ingredients, lets editors publish it with a provenance label. A manifest naming a generative tool, or a hash that no longer matches, sends it to forensic review, and an image with no credentials is treated as of unknown origin, not as authentic.

An insurer's claims app lets assessors apply an AI tool that enhances and annotates photographs of vehicle damage, and records each AI edit as an action in the photograph's manifest. When a claim is disputed, a reviewing assessor or the claimant's representative can see which changes the AI tool made and check them against the retained original, which the edited photograph's manifest cites as an ingredient.

A social-media platform reads Content Credentials on upload, labels images whose trusted manifest declares a generative AI source, and shows users who signed the record. Its trust-and-safety team tracks what share of uploads carry trusted, untrusted or no credentials, to decide how far its synthetic-media policy can rely on the labels and where it still needs other detection methods.

limitations.description: The record is easy to lose. Anyone can remove the manifest, an attack the C2PA's own threat model expects, and the file is then an ordinary file with no link to its history unless a watermark or fingerprint soft binding was registered with a manifest repository. Because credentials are optional and removable, a file without them says nothing about its origin: the absence of a manifest cannot show that content is human-made or unaltered.

A valid manifest shows who signed the record and that what its hash covers is unchanged, not that its statements are true. A signer can omit an AI step, a stolen key yields manifests that validate, and a camera photographing a screen signs a genuine capture of a staged scene. Validators need not check revocation, metadata such as location may sit outside the hash, and a 2026 preprint found validators disagreeing on the same file, so a result depends on the signer, validator and trust list.

The history is complete only while every tool in the workflow supports C2PA. An edit made in an unsupported tool is not recorded, and if the file later passes through a supporting tool, the new signer implicitly vouches for that unrecorded change, so the chain can show fewer steps than took place. The C2PA itself says the approach depends on widespread adoption by tools and platforms.

Manifests can disclose more than the creator intends, such as capture time and place, device details, the edit history and, through the separate Creator Assertions Working Group identity extension, who made the content. The C2PA's threat model lists identifying creators and tracking viewers as risks. Assertions can be redacted when a file is reused as an ingredient, but people working in risky settings, such as human-rights documentation, must decide what to include before signing.

Support for AI-generated text is immature. Embedding a manifest in plain text, as invisible Unicode characters, entered the specification in version 2.3 and is still marked as under review; the reference SDK supports it only behind an unstable option, and any edit to the text breaks the hash. For language-model output the method is much less dependable than for images, video and audio, where embedding is established.

techniques.name: Zero-Knowledge Proof of Model Inference
techniques.description: A zero-knowledge proof of model inference lets the owner of a model show an outside party that one specific model, fixed in advance, turns a particular input into a particular output, without revealing the model's weights. The owner publishes a commitment to the weights, a short cryptographic fingerprint such as a hash that binds them without disclosing them, together with a verification key that fixes the model's architecture. The model's arithmetic is converted to whole numbers (quantised) and written as a system of equations called a circuit, and for each input a proving system produces a proof, of a few kilobytes to a few hundred kilobytes, that this circuit, run with weights matching the commitment, turns that input into that output; the input can be public or committed in the same way. Anyone holding the verification key can check the proof in milliseconds to seconds: it shows that the committed model gives that output for that input, while keeping the weights hidden, and says nothing about whether that model is accurate, fair or safe. Unlike homomorphic encryption, which lets a server compute on data it cannot read but gives the caller no evidence of which computation was run, and unlike model signing, which lets someone who holds a model's files check who released them, it lets someone who never sees the weights check individual outputs against them.

example_use_cases.description: A credit-scoring vendor publishes the weight commitment in the report of an independent bias and accuracy audit, which was run on the quantised model bound to that commitment. When a refused applicant complains, the lender's complaints team asks the vendor for a proof for that decision and checks it against the published commitment, to confirm that the audited model gives the same refusal on the applicant's data before it reviews the decision itself.

A hospital trust buying chest X-ray triage results from a cloud provider writes into the contract that its clinical engineering team may challenge a random sample of each month's results. For each sampled case the provider must return a proof against the commitment to the model the trust validated, and the team treats a failed or missing proof as evidence that a different model was served, which triggers the contract's audit clause.

An online-safety regulator inspecting the age-estimation service a platform relies on submits its own test images and asks for a proof with each estimate. Its inspectors check each proof against the commitment registered when an accredited laboratory certified the vendor's model, to decide whether the service in use is the certified model, without the vendor handing its proprietary weights to the regulator.

limitations.description: A valid proof shows that the committed weights turn this input into this output. It does not show that the model is accurate, fair or safe, that the input was genuine, or that the service ran the committed model: a different model giving the same output passes too, so spot checks catch a substituted model only on inputs where the two disagree. A commitment carries assurance only if an audit was run on the model it binds.

Proving costs far more than running the model. Published figures: 88 seconds per prediction of a 15-million-parameter VGG16 on CIFAR-10 images (zkCNN), about 41 minutes for an ImageNet-scale MobileNet on a large cloud server (Kang et al.), and about 13 minutes for one 2,048-token pass of a 13-billion-parameter language model on a data-centre GPU, after a one-off 16-minute commitment (zkLLM). Proving every output of a busy service is impractical, so protocols prove sampled or disputed outputs.

The proof covers a quantised, whole-number version of the model, not the floating-point model that was trained and perhaps audited, and the two can give slightly different outputs. Published attacks plant backdoors that stay dormant at full precision and activate only after quantisation, which EZKL's security notes flag. Audits and accuracy tests must therefore be run on the quantised model that is actually proved, or the commitment and the audit describe different models.

The guarantee depends on configuration. If the weights are private inputs with no published commitment, a proof shows only that some weights for the stated architecture give the output. Hashing the weights inside the proof keeps them hidden but costs about as much again as proving the inference. EZKL's cheaper settings, including its Python default, bind the weights without fully hiding them, and its notes warn they can be recovered from enough proofs. The architecture is normally disclosed.

Soundness rests on the software as well as the mathematics. A compiler error that leaves the equations under-constrained can let a false proof verify, a risk EZKL's documentation names, and EZKL's proofs rely on public parameters from a multi-party set-up ceremony. Audits cover specific releases (EZKL's covered version 21), so verifiers should fix which tool versions and parameters they accept. EZKL, the most used tool, has had no open-source licence since January 2024.
